html:
Aboriginal Tasmanians are the first people of Tasmania, the island south of mainland Australia. They appear on the maps for 3000 BCE, 1783 and 1800, before and just as British settlers arrived.

Their ancestors walked to Tasmania over dry land tens of thousands of years ago. Around 6000 BCE the sea rose and filled Bass Strait, cutting the island off. For some eight thousand years they lived apart from the rest of the world, in several nations with their own languages. They hunted wallabies and seals, gathered shellfish, used fire to manage the land and crossed rivers in bark canoes. See also Tasmanian hunter-gatherers.

Abel Tasman sighted the island in 1642, and Britain settled it in 1803. Settlers seized hunting grounds, and the Black War of the 1820s left most of the people dead. George Augustus Robinson moved the survivors to Flinders Island, where many more died. Truganini, who died in 1876, was long wrongly called the last of them. Thousands of descendants, many from families on the Bass Strait islands, live in Tasmania today and are reviving a language, palawa kani.
sum: Aboriginal Tasmanians are the first people of Tasmania, the island south of mainland Australia. They appear on the maps for 3000 BCE, 1783 and 1800, before and just as British settlers arrived.
